newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania sees no energy crisis this winter.
newsitem.headline: Romania sees no energy crisis this winter.

text.p: Romania's Industry Ministry on Wednesday dismissed rumours that the country might face a repeat of the energy crisis it suffered last winter.

"Rumours of an alleged energy crisis in Romania...have no real basis. Their sole motivation is to induce a state of anxiety among the people, suitable only for electoral games," state secretary Lucian Motiu told a news conference.
Romania holds parliamentary and presidential elections on November 3.

On Tuesday the country's big trade unions said electricity authority Renel RA, unable to collect unpaid bills worth hundreds of millions of dollars, would fail to secure the fuel supplies its power plants will need in the coming winter.
Motiu said a programme to build up energy reserves was going smoothly.

"Activities to set up reserves for winter are in full swing and so far more than 5.0 million tonnes of coal and around 900 million cubic metres of gas have been stored," he said, adding that the process would be completed by mid-October.

"As far as oil imports are concerned, we have had good signs from Georgia and Iran. We hope to get 2.0 million tonnes of crude under a contract with Iran," said Romanian Oil Company (CRP) manager Mihai Georgescu.
Motiu said the government would guarantee a $160 million loan for fuel oil imports by Renel, as well as $200 million for crude imports by the CRP.
"We will annually import some 10 million tonnes of crude, 4.0 million tonnes of fuel oil and 7.0 billion cubic metres of (natural) gas," Motiu said.
Romania annually produces around 6.6 million tonnes of crude and some 20 billion cubic metres of gas.
Last winter, an acute shortage of hard currency to pay for fuel imports forced Renel to cut power supplies to Romania's industrial sectors over January-March.

Last month, in a bid to avoid a repeat of the crisis, the government created a special fund for energy imports by forcing some 100 state-run companies to exchange their hard currency earnings at the disadvantageous official rate.

On Wednesday, Romanian central bank governor Mugur Isarescu backtracked on the measure, saying most companies would no longer contribute. Loans and privatisation earnings would continue to be paid into the fund.
The central bank move seemed a response to a plunge in credibility abroad that was hampering attempts to raise loans on the international market.
